analysis.one_liner: Adds dental coverage to Medicare, Medicaid, ACA plans, and veterans' care, and funds dental clinics and training.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to committee, where it died without a hearing or vote; it had one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add dental care—including preventive work, dentures, and emergency treatment—as a covered benefit under Medicare and Medicaid, and require insurance sold under the Affordable Care Act to cover it for adults as well as children. It would also require the Department of Veterans Affairs to provide dental care like any other medical service, and fund dental clinics in schools, mobile clinics, dental residencies, and loan repayment to build the dental workforce in underserved areas. It was referred to the Senate health committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, adults on Medicaid, pregnant women, veterans, prisoners, and people served by tribal and community health programs would gain coverage for dental care that most of them currently pay for out of pocket or go without. Children and adults in marketplace plans would gain dental coverage as a required benefit. Community health centers, dental schools, and dental hygienists and therapists would gain new federal funding and expanded roles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, Medicaid enrollees, veterans, underserved communities

how_it_helps.text: Adds comprehensive oral health services—including preventive, restorative, emergency, and denture care—to Medicare, with preventive care covered at 100% and other care at 80%.

Defines oral health services as a required Medicaid benefit for adults, including pregnant and postpartum women, and gives states a 15-percentage-point boost in the federal share for dental spending if they pay providers at least 70% of usual and customary fees.
Makes oral health services an essential health benefit for children and adults in ACA marketplace plans, and requires VA to furnish dental care like any other medical service.

Funds the dental workforce: National Health Service Corps scholarships and loan repayment for dentists and dental therapists, community-based dental residencies, dental clinics in schools, mobile dental services, and alternative provider programs for veterans, prisoners, and Indian Health Service communities.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally, through federal spending: Medicare would pay for dental services for seniors, the federal share of Medicaid dental costs would rise 15 percentage points, and new grant, scholarship, and loan repayment programs would be funded. States would share the Medicaid cost. Dental insurers in the marketplace market would bear new coverage requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state taxpayers; dental insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill is an expensive entitlement expansion: it adds dental care to Medicare with 80-100% federal payment and raises the federal Medicaid match by 15 percentage points for dental spending, and most of its program funding is authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary'—open-ended spending with no dedicated revenue source.

Reimbursement floors and expanded coverage could strain an already short dental workforce, and Medicaid states must pay providers at least 70% of usual and customary fees to qualify for the enhanced match, which could pressure state budgets to add their own spending.

Expanded coverage routes new public spending through existing dental providers and private plans (oral health becomes an essential health benefit covering adults), so part of the benefit flows to provider and insurance revenues as well as to patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—covering dental care for seniors, Medicaid enrollees, and veterans—are large and well-documented: untreated dental disease drives pain, infection, and expensive emergency-room visits that taxpayers end up paying anyway. The costs are real: the federal government would take on significant new spending for Medicare dental benefits and higher Medicaid matching funds, and taxpayers bear that bill. The bill was an aspirational full expansion without a financing mechanism attached, which is partly why it attracted almost no cosponsors. But since it never even got a committee hearing, the merits were never weighed in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 16, 2024 and read twice in the Senate.
The same day it was referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions—the only action after introduction.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill never advanced past committee; it died with no further action.
It had one cosponsor in the Senate, giving it no visible bloc of support to push committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome preserved the status quo: existing dental providers keep their current mix of private-pay and limited public reimbursement, and no new federal dental spending was committed. Seniors, Medicaid adults, and veterans without dental coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo kept; no new federal dental spending

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action—hearing, markup, or report—leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic cosponsor and a single Independent sponsor; no vote was ever taken, and no Republican signed on, so no party-line pattern can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would bring tens of millions of Medicare and Medicaid patients into coverage with required payment floors (at least 70% of usual and customary fees in Medicaid), greatly expanding paid patient volume. Its stance runs alongside the public's interest in access, though providers also gain revenue from the expansion.

The bill adds oral health to the ACA essential health benefits, creating a much larger covered market for dental plans while subjecting them to federal benefit standards. Expanded coverage would mainly benefit patients, not the insurers' existing position.

The bill creates new open-ended federal obligations: Medicare dental payment, a 15-point higher federal Medicaid match, and multiple grant and workforce programs. That cost lands on the general taxpayer, offset partly by reduced emergency-room dental visits.
